Köppen-Geiger climate matching of plant pests against Norway

Method, data and worked examples behind kg_viewer

Author

Daniel Flø

Published

November 3, 2026

Code 
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(terra)
library(rnaturalearth)

DB <- "../kg_climate.db"
q  <- function(sql, params = NULL) {
  con <- dbConnect(SQLite(), DB, flags = SQLITE_RO)
  on.exit(dbDisconnect(con))
  dbGetQuery(con, sql, params = params)
}

build   <- with(q("SELECT * FROM buildInfo"), setNames(value, key))
legend  <- q("SELECT * FROM kgLegend ORDER BY kgValue")
kg_cols <- setNames(legend$hex, legend$kgCode)
species <- q("SELECT * FROM species")

source("../R/support.R")        # data-support levels and tints, shared with the app
source("../R/support_map.R")
source("../R/support_bins.R")

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
            theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
                  plot.title.position = "plot"))

1 Purpose

To establish, a pest that arrives in Norway has to survive and reproduce in the climate it lands in. Pest risk ranking models therefore ask an establishment question about climate suitability, for example EST1 in FinnPRIO (Heikkilä et al. 2016). Assessors usually answer it by hand, from distribution maps and expert knowledge.

kg_viewer supplies the evidence for that judgement. It does this in a consistent and documented way that can be repeated for many species. For each pest it answers three questions:

  1. Which Köppen-Geiger climate classes does the pest demonstrably occupy?
  2. How much of non-alpine Norway lies in those classes today?
  3. How does that share change under a high-emission scenario for 2041–2070?

The current build (2026-11-03) covers 62 species and 70,456 occupied 1 km cells.

2 Where this sits among climate-matching methods

Pest risk assessments use climate in roughly three ways, from simplest to most demanding:

Approach Example Needs Output
Climate classification overlay Köppen-Geiger classes of the known range vs. the risk area Occurrences Shared classes, area share
Process-based niche models CLIMEX (Sutherst and Maywald 1985) Occurrences plus physiology (thresholds, diapause) Ecoclimatic index
Correlative species distribution models MaxEnt, GLM/GAM ensembles (Elith and Leathwick 2009) Occurrences, background, covariates Continuous suitability

Overlaying Köppen-Geiger classes is the standard first screen in EU pest categorisation. EFSA’s Plant Health Panel compares the classes in a pest’s range with those in the EU (EFSA Panel on Plant Health (PLH) 2018). The method is coarse, but it is transparent, cheap, and easy to defend in an assessment text, and it works for species with only tens of records, where SDMs are unreliable. Baker et al. (2000) discuss its strengths and pitfalls for non-indigenous pests.

kg_viewer keeps this approach and fixes several weaknesses of how it is usually applied:

  • Resolution. It uses the 1 km Beck et al. maps (Beck et al. 2023) instead of the 0.5° Kottek map (Kottek et al. 2006). Coastal and mountain gradients, which shape Norway’s climate, are resolved.
  • Data cleaning. GBIF records are filtered and screened with CoordinateCleaner (Zizka et al. 2019) before any class is counted.
  • Thresholded occupancy. A class counts only with enough independent cells (rule below), not because of a single record. EFSA practice is unthresholded.
  • Explicit uncertainty. A resampling test reports whether the Norway-relevant class list would change with half the data. Each occupied class also carries a data-support level (its cell count), shown directly on the map.
  • Future climate. The same classes are evaluated against Norway’s 2041–2070 SSP5-8.5 map from the same, internally consistent dataset.

3 Data

3.1 Climate: Beck et al. 2023

The maps cover 1901–2099 at 1 km. Future periods use an ensemble of CMIP6 models constrained by observed warming (Beck et al. 2023). This build uses Beck et al. 2023, Scientific Data, 1991-2020 for classifying occurrences and Norway, and 2041-2070, SSP5-8.5 for Norway’s future profile.

Norway is measured by area (km², with cell area shrinking with latitude). The alpine/polar classes ET, EF are excluded because practically no plant pests establish there, so all shares are of non-alpine Norway.

Code 
no <- bind_rows(
  q("SELECT * FROM kgNorway")       |> mutate(period = "1991–2020"),
  q("SELECT * FROM kgNorwayFuture") |> mutate(period = "2041–2070 SSP5-8.5")
) |>
  left_join(legend, by = "kgCode") |>
  mutate(kgCode = reorder(kgCode, -proportion, max))

ggplot(no, aes(kgCode, proportion, fill = kgCode, alpha = period)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(0.8), width = 0.75, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(proportion, 0.1)),
            position = position_dodge(0.8), vjust = -0.3, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = kg_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_alpha_manual(values = c(1, 0.45), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = expansion(c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Norway's climate profile, now and in 2041–2070") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

Norway today is dominated by the cold-summer boreal class Dfc. Under SSP5-8.5 it gives way to the warm-summer Dfb and the oceanic Cfb. A pest whose occupied classes include Dfb or Cfb therefore gains ground in Norway over time. One restricted to warmer classes does not, because those classes do not appear in Norway at all.

Code 
shift <- full_join(q("SELECT kgCode, proportion AS now FROM kgNorway"),
                   q("SELECT kgCode, proportion AS future FROM kgNorwayFuture"),
                   by = "kgCode") |>
  mutate(across(c(now, future), ~ coalesce(.x, 0)),
         change = future - now) |>
  left_join(select(legend, kgCode, kgLabel), by = "kgCode") |>
  arrange(desc(now))

knitr::kable(transmute(shift, Class = kgCode, Climate = kgLabel,
                       `1991–2020` = scales::percent(now, 0.01),
                       `2041–2070` = scales::percent(future, 0.01),
                       `Change (pp)` = sprintf("%+.1f", 100 * change)))

3.2 Occurrences: GBIF

Records come from one GBIF occurrence download for all species (rgbif::occ_download), using the accepted backbone key of each species: GBIF.org (2026-11-03) GBIF Occurrence Download https://doi.org/10.15468/dl.23jhbx. Only records with coordinates, no geospatial issue and status PRESENT are kept. Cleaning is fully recorded in buildInfo:

Step Setting
Basis of record dropped FOSSIL_SPECIMEN, LIVING_SPECIMEN
Max. coordinate uncertainty 10000 m (missing kept)
CoordinateCleaner tests capitals, centroids, equal, gbif, institutions, zeros

After cleaning, records are thinned to one per 1 km raster cell. This is the unit everything is counted in. It removes much of the sampling bias that comes from many records at one well-visited site, though not all of it (see Limitations).

Code 
funnel <- species |>
  select(eppoCode, Downloaded = nDownloaded, Cleaned = nClean, `1 km cells` = nCells) |>
  pivot_longer(-eppoCode, names_to = "stage") |>
  mutate(stage = factor(stage, c("Downloaded", "Cleaned", "1 km cells")))

ggplot(funnel, aes(stage, value, group = eppoCode)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.35, colour = "steelblue4") +
  geom_point(size = 1, colour = "steelblue4") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "From GBIF download to counted cells")
Code 
tot <- colSums(species[, c("nDownloaded", "nClean", "nCells")])

Across all species, 151,867 downloaded records become 147,816 after cleaning, which thin to 70,456 cells.

3.3 Host trees: Caudullo et al. 2017

As context for the climate evidence, the app can draw the natural range of a pest’s host trees as a dashed outline over the climate map. The climate shading itself never changes with the host. Ranges come from the chorological maps for the main European woody species (Caudullo et al. 2017), which map each species’ whole natural range. Host lists come from the EPPO Global Database. host_db.R adds them to the database after kg_db.R:

  • Exact species matches only. A host counts when its EPPO name equals one of the 104 mapped species. Genus entries (“Pinus”) and subspecies or varieties are not matched. Host types kept: Major host, Host, Wild/Weed.
  • Natural range only. Per map part the coast-clipped polygons, else the unclipped ones, plus isolated populations (drawn as 10 km discs). Planted or naturalised occurrences are not used.
  • One range at a time. Each host on its own, or all hosts of the pest combined.
Code 
host_cov <- q("SELECT eppoCode, COUNT(*) AS n FROM pestHosts GROUP BY eppoCode")

18 of 62 species have at least one mapped host. Most of the rest are crop pests, or pests of North American and Asian trees, whose hosts are not among the European species.

4 From occurrences to evidence

4.1 The occupancy rule

A class is occupied by a species when it holds

\[ n_k \ge 5 \quad\text{and}\quad n_k \ge 0.1\,\% \times \sum_j n_j \]

where \(n_k\) is the number of the species’ 1 km cells in class \(k\). The absolute floor removes single misplaced, mislabelled or interception records. The relative floor matters for widespread species, where a few hundred residual errors could otherwise pass the absolute floor. No published standard exists for these thresholds. They are judgement values and are stored with the data so they can be challenged and changed.

The rule is implemented as the SQL view occupiedKgClasses. The raw counts in pestKgClasses remain unfiltered, so any other rule can be applied downstream.

4.2 Norway overlap

The headline number is the share of non-alpine Norway lying in the occupied classes:

\[ \text{pctNorway} = \sum_{k \in \text{occupied}} \frac{A_{\text{Norway},k}}{A_{\text{Norway}}} \]

Code 
overlap <- q("
  SELECT s.eppoCode, s.scientificName, s.nCellsNonAlpine AS cells,
         s.uncertainty, s.classStability,
         COALESCE((SELECT SUM(n.proportion) FROM occupiedKgClasses o
                   JOIN kgNorway n USING (kgCode) WHERE o.eppoCode = s.eppoCode), 0) AS now,
         COALESCE((SELECT SUM(f.proportion) FROM occupiedKgClasses o
                   JOIN kgNorwayFuture f USING (kgCode) WHERE o.eppoCode = s.eppoCode), 0) AS future
  FROM species s") |>
  mutate(uncertainty = factor(uncertainty, c("low", "medium", "high")))
Code 
unc_cols <- c(low = "#1b7837", medium = "#e08214", high = "#b2182b")

ggplot(overlap, aes(y = reorder(scientificName, pmax(now, future)))) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = now, xend = future, yend = reorder(scientificName, pmax(now, future))),
               colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(aes(x = now, colour = uncertainty), shape = 21, size = 2, stroke = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(x = future, colour = uncertainty), size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unc_cols, name = "Uncertainty") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Share of non-alpine Norway in occupied classes", y = NULL,
       title = "Climate overlap with Norway, all species") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(face = "italic", size = 8),
        legend.position = "top")
Code 
grp <- overlap |>
  mutate(group = case_when(now > 0.5 ~ "dfc",
                           now == 0 & future == 0 ~ "none",
                           future > now ~ "rising",
                           TRUE ~ "falling")) |>
  count(group) |>
  with(setNames(n, group))

The species fall into three groups:

  • 7 species occupy Dfc and overlap with more than half of Norway already.
  • 32 species occupy Dfb and/or Cfb but not Dfc. Their overlap is modest today and grows by mid-century as those classes expand.
  • 17 species have 0 % in both periods. They are restricted to classes absent from non-alpine Norway, so the Köppen-Geiger evidence argues against establishment outdoors.

A further 6 species share only marginal classes with Norway today, such as the subpolar oceanic Cfc. Those classes all but disappear by 2041–2070, so a warmer climate does not automatically mean a higher overlap.

4.3 Supporting indicators

The species table carries further evidence an assessor can cite:

Column Meaning
nCellsNorway, nCellsNordic, nordicCountries Cells already recorded in Norway or the Nordic countries (NO, SE, FI)
nCellsEurope Cells in Europe (Russia west of 60° E)
lat95 95th percentile of absolute latitude of occupied-class cells, a poleward edge robust to stray points
borealOccupied Whether any cold-summer class (Dfc, Dfd, Dwc, Dwd, Dsc, Dsd) is occupied
pctCellsSince2000 Share of cells with a record since 2000, which flags ranges known only from old data

4.4 Uncertainty: class stability

More records could reveal further occupied classes, so a class list from 30 cells is less trustworthy than one from 20,000. To quantify this, the pipeline draws 100 random halves of each species’ cells. It applies the occupancy rule to each half, with the absolute floor halved, and records how often the occupied classes that occur in Norway match the full-data result. Instability in a tropical class does not matter for Norway, so it is ignored.

The rating combines stability with sample size:

  • low: ≥ 2000 cells and stability ≥ 0.9
  • medium: ≥ 200 cells and stability ≥ 0.5
  • high: everything else
Code 
ggplot(overlap, aes(cells, classStability, colour = uncertainty)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(build[c("uncMediumCells", "uncLowCells")]),
             linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0.5, 0.9), linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unc_cols, name = "Uncertainty") +
  labs(x = "Non-alpine 1 km cells (log)", y = "Class stability",
       title = "How robust is each class list?")
Code 
knitr::kable(count(overlap, uncertainty, name = "Species"))
uncertainty Species
low 4
medium 20
high 38

The many high ratings are expected. Most quarantine pests are rare in GBIF, which is part of why they are quarantine pests. For these species, the Köppen-Geiger evidence should be weighed lightly against literature on thermal requirements.

4.5 Data support per class

The stability rating covers the species as a whole, but within one species the occupied classes can rest on very different amounts of data. A class with 486 cells and a class with 21 cells both count as occupied. Each occupied class therefore also gets a data support level, taken directly from its number of 1 km cells. No model is involved, only counts already in pestKgClasses.

How many levels, and where to break? I compared 3, 4 and 5 levels, each with two kinds of breaks:

  • Quantile: equal numbers of classes per level.
  • Fisher natural breaks: the partition that best separates log cell counts.

Each break set is also tested rounded to readable numbers. Two scores decide between them:

  • GVF (goodness of variance fit): how well the levels separate the counts, where 1 is perfect.
  • Stability: each species’ cells are resampled 500 times, and stability is the share of resamples in which a class keeps its level. Dropping below the occupancy rule counts as a change. The same score is also reported for Norway’s three main classes alone, along with the stability of the weakest level.
Code 
bins <- compare_support_bins(DB, B = 500)
bins |>
  mutate(across(c(GVF, stability, stabNorway, weakestLevel), ~ round(.x, 2))) |>
  rename(Levels = levels, Method = method, `Breaks (cells)` = breaks,
         Stability = stability, `Stability (Dfc/Dfb/Cfb)` = stabNorway,
         `Weakest level` = weakestLevel, `Classes per level` = perLevel) |>
  knitr::kable()
Levels Method Breaks (cells) GVF Stability Stability (Dfc/Dfb/Cfb) Weakest level Classes per level

Code 
ggplot(bins, aes(stability, GVF, colour = factor(levels), shape = sub(" rounded", "", method))) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = filter(bins, method == "fisher rounded"),
            aes(label = breaks), hjust = -0.08, size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(c(0.05, 0.45))) +
  labs(x = "Stability under resampling", y = "Separation (GVF)",
       colour = "Levels", shape = "Breaks",
       title = "Choosing the data-support levels")

Fisher breaks beat quantiles at every number of levels, on both scores. Quantile levels slice the crowded low end (5–20 cells) thinly, and classes flip between them easily. More levels separate better but are less stable. Five levels also leave only 9 classes in the top level.

Three levels with rounded Fisher breaks keep stability around 0.90 while separating far better than two:

  • high: 200 or more cells;
  • medium: 25–199 cells;
  • low: 5–24 cells.

These values are set in R/support.R and used by the app and these documents. Classes under 5 cells are not occupied and get no level.

Code 
occ_all <- q("SELECT kgCode, nCells FROM occupiedKgClasses") |>
  mutate(support = factor(SUPPORT_NAMES[support_level(nCells)], SUPPORT_NAMES))
ggplot(occ_all, aes(nCells, fill = support)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, boundary = log10(5), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = SUPPORT_BREAKS, linetype = 2, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = tint("#2c7fb8", SUPPORT_TINT), name = "Data support") +
  labs(x = "Cells in the class (log scale)", y = "Occupied classes")

On maps, data support is drawn as a tint: each class keeps its Köppen-Geiger colour, mixed with 45 % or 72 % white for medium or low support. The legend is a grid of classes against support levels, like a bivariate map legend.

The levels count cells, not independent sites. Thirty cells from one survey weigh the same as thirty cells spread over a continent.

5 Worked example

Code 
EPPO <- "LYMAMA"
sp   <- filter(overlap, eppoCode == EPPO)
pts  <- q("SELECT * FROM occurrences WHERE eppoCode = ?", list(EPPO))
cls  <- q("SELECT p.kgCode, p.nCells, o.kgCode IS NOT NULL AS occupied,
                  n.proportion AS norway, f.proportion AS norwayFuture
           FROM pestKgClasses p
           LEFT JOIN occupiedKgClasses o USING (eppoCode, kgCode)
           LEFT JOIN kgNorway n USING (kgCode)
           LEFT JOIN kgNorwayFuture f USING (kgCode)
           WHERE p.eppoCode = ? ORDER BY p.nCells DESC", list(EPPO))

Lymantria mathura (LYMAMA) has 1,394 cleaned cells and a class stability of 0.84, which gives an uncertainty rating of medium.

Code 
support_map(DB, "../koppen_geiger_0p1.tif", EPPO, title = FALSE)
Code 
cls |>
  left_join(select(legend, kgCode, kgLabel), by = "kgCode") |>
  transmute(Class = kgCode, Climate = kgLabel, Cells = nCells,
            Occupied = if_else(occupied == 1, "✓", ""),
            Support = if_else(occupied == 1, SUPPORT_NAMES[support_level(nCells)], ""),
            `Norway 1991–2020` = scales::percent(coalesce(norway, 0), 0.1),
            `Norway 2041–2070` = scales::percent(coalesce(norwayFuture, 0), 0.1)) |>
  knitr::kable()

In the occupied classes this gives an overlap of 24.0% of non-alpine Norway today and 42.5% in 2041–2070. The two shares do not rest on equal data. Dfb has medium support (115 cells), while Cfb, which covers Norway’s west coast, has low support (21 cells). An EST1 justification could cite the shared classes, their area and their data support. It should also check lat95 (43.3°) and any Nordic records (0 cells) as supporting evidence.

To reproduce this for another species, change EPPO above or pick the species in the app.

6 Limitations

  • Classes are coarse. One Köppen-Geiger class spans a wide range of winter minima and degree-days. Dfc in Siberia and Dfc on the Norwegian coast differ in exactly the variables (frost severity, season length) that often limit pests. A shared class means not excluded, not suitable.
  • The realised range understates the fundamental niche. A pest absent from a class may be limited by dispersal, hosts or recent arrival rather than climate. Shares are therefore conservative for spreading invaders, and the pctCellsSince2000 column helps to flag them.
  • Sampling bias persists. Thinning to 1 km does not correct for whole regions being under-sampled, such as much of Asia and Africa in GBIF. Classes typical of poorly sampled regions are under-represented.
  • Protected cultivation. MANAGED records are dropped, but greenhouse populations are often not flagged in GBIF. Some records in cold classes may be glasshouse records.
  • Taxonomy. Pathovars and other infraspecific taxa missing from the GBIF backbone are skipped rather than resolved to the species, which would inflate the range. Synonym resolution depends on the GBIF backbone.
  • Host ranges are partial context. Only hosts among the European species of Caudullo et al. (2017) are mapped, matched by exact name, so a pest’s other hosts (and planted trees outside the natural range) are missing. Ranges are present-day, also when the 2041–2070 climate map is shown.
  • One scenario. SSP5-8.5 is a high-end scenario and is used here as a reasonable worst case, not a forecast.
  • Thresholds are judgements. The occupancy rule and uncertainty cut-offs are explicit and stored in buildInfo, but they are not calibrated against known establishment outcomes. Validation against pests with documented establishment or failure in Fennoscandia is the obvious next step.

For high-stakes assessments, follow up a large Norway overlap with process-based modelling (CLIMEX) or a correlative SDM on bioclimatic variables. Both use the cleaned, thinned records in occurrences as their starting point.

The database is rebuilt with kg_db.R. GBIF downloads are cached per species in gbif_cache/, so a rebuild with different thresholds needs no network access. Host ranges are then added with host_db.R (EPPO host lists cached in eppo_cache/; Caudullo shapefiles in data/shp/cho, not in the repository). Render this vignette from the vignettes/ folder with quarto render kg_viewer.qmd.
